prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms enabled spectroscopy at a fractional uncertainty near 1e-18

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B014 as a single-achievement prize for Katori and Ye, and the exchange sharpened rather than weakened the case. The question the chair put to Lindroth, Johansson and me, whether the lattice clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, has a one-sentence answer that I would put in the citation: the comb is a frequency ruler that makes optical oscillations countable, the ion prize is about control of one quantum system at a time, while the lattice clock is the idea that a trapping potential can be made to leave a forbidden optical transition unshifted (magic wavelength, Lamb-Dicke regime), so that very many neutral atoms are interrogated at once with Doppler and recoil shifts removed and quantum projection noise cut by the atom number. That is a different mechanism and a different measurement, and it has been verified by what I regard as the decisive test in my own field, namely independent clocks in several laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST and others) agreeing at the 1e-18 level. The scientific claim is therefore established now and does not depend on the CGPM timetable for redefining the second. The credit maps onto the physics: Katori proposed the scheme and Ye's group brought it to the performance frontier and to the redshift and many-body measurements. I would keep the citation limited to invention and realization at that level of uncertainty and not promise geodesy or dark-matter results, which are still mostly projected.
statement.case_against: The reservations that all six of us on B014 share remain real and I do not think round 1 removed them. First, a critic can read this as a third prize in precision time after 1989, 2005 and 2012; I think the distinction above answers that, but it is a judgement and not a proof. Second, the credit omits Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Takamoto and others, and the chair is right that several of us, myself included, are working from recalled priority dates (Katori's magic-wavelength proposal in 2001-2003, the first strontium lattice demonstrations after it) and have not checked them against papers. If the dates did not support Katori as originator, I would change my view of the two-name credit. Third, my own bias toward metrology is real: I rank measurement techniques high by temperament, and Danielsson and Eriksson are entitled to ask whether I am rewarding an instrument. My answer is that a prize for an instrument is right when it opens measurements nobody could make before, and the clock-to-clock comparisons at 1e-18 are such measurements, but I accept that this is a criterion on which reasonable members differ.

responses.point: Lindroth is asked by the chair to say whether she would defend the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and she argues the Lamb-Dicke and magic-wavelength mechanism makes it a single explanatory idea.
responses.response: I would defend the distinction in the same terms and I think it can be put in one sentence for the citation: neutral atoms in a magic-wavelength lattice are interrogated as a large ensemble with the trapping shifts cancelled by design, which neither the comb nor ion control provides. I would ask her, since she is closest to the field, to check the 2001-2003 dates for Katori's proposal and the first strontium lattice demonstration against the literature, as Olsson also requests, because the claim of originator rests on it. I also agree with her that the wording should stay at the level of invention and realization.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B021 because nature supplied the diffuse neutrino flux, argues that waiting for the SI redefinition costs the clock nothing, and asks whether pioneers should be honoured while they are alive and active.
responses.response: I take the discovery-versus-instrument argument seriously and the diffuse flux is secure; I said so in round 1. But waiting does cost something I care about: the redefinition is an administrative decision that follows from the clock science and is not a condition of it, and tying a scientific prize to the CGPM schedule would be a poor reason to defer. On B021, the confirmation is across IceCube analysis channels, not across detectors, and your own file concedes KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are not yet comparable; the three-name cut among Halzen, Karle and Spiering with DUMAND, Baikal and AMANDA behind them is also less settled than Katori and Ye. You asked what would move you, and I would ask the same of myself: an expert note showing independent detector confirmation and a credit history that fixes the names would make B021 a strong prize, and I have moved it into my alternatives for that reason.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B016 for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a new class of matter confirmed by quantised edge transport, admits the credit gap around Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 2016 overlap, and asks whether the clock is an instrument or a discovery.
responses.response: I accept that the clock is an enabling instrument in his sense and I do not claim a measurement technique outranks a new state of matter in general; the distinction I rely on is that this one has produced new measured results (gravitational redshift across millimetre heights, many-body clock effects, bounds on constants). On B016 I see the Z2 invariant, edge states and the HgTe conductance measurement as distinct from the 2016 prize and the experimental confirmation by transport and ARPES is strong. My problem is the one you state yourself: the experiment rewarded tested a prediction by people outside the three names, one of whom has died, and I cannot defend that credit as cleanly as Katori and Ye. I therefore keep B016 as my first alternative and would support it if the committee judged that conceptual weight outweighed tidiness of attribution.

responses.point: Olsson ranked B042 first but now places it below B014 because the STEM corrector side (Krivanek) is missing, electron microscopy already has Ruska 1986 and cryo-EM 2017, and she asks that Katori's dates be checked before the citation is fixed.
responses.response: I agree with her request on the dates and with the disclosure that she would step back on B042; I think that is the right handling. Her point on credit is also the one I made in round 1: the corrector story has a TEM branch and a STEM branch and the three names cover only one. I would add that I want to see enabled physics and not only better images, and she supplies the physics-versus-chemistry question that I had not weighed. I would not move B042 into my alternatives.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, supports B014 after moving from IceCube, flags that agreement is partly the result of members moving toward it, and says he relies on others for the clock priority history.
responses.response: The chair's observation that the consensus on B014 is partly convergent and not independent is fair and I try to apply it to myself: Lindroth and I are in neighbouring fields and both declared the bias. That is a reason to ask for a checked priority history by someone not in the clock community, not a reason to change the science. I agree with him that a two-part configuration adding B021 or B008 cannot respect the three-person limit, so the final choice is among single-achievement prizes, and that Spiering's inclusion in any IceCube credit, as Olsson argues, would not leave room beside Katori and Ye.

responses.point: Johansson prefers B014, concedes he may be rating the safest option highly, and wants the citation to say invention and realisation so that it does not read as credit for the whole community.
responses.response: I agree with that wording and have revised my citation to name the lattice clock and the magic-wavelength mechanism, and to state the 1e-18 uncertainty as the realization, without listing applications. On B009 your own disclosure and your doubts about timing after the 2025 prize match mine, and I have not carried B009 or my earlier B008 into the alternatives: B008 overlaps Wineland's 2012 prize more than I earlier allowed, and splitting four names would also break the limit.

uncertainties: I have recalled, not checked, the priority chronology of Katori's magic-wavelength proposal versus the first lattice demonstrations and the Ye group's record uncertainties; an independent check would settle whether Katori and Ye are the right pair.
Whether the committee accepts the distinction from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which I regard as defensible but not certain.
Whether Danielsson and Eriksson regard the clock as an instrument that should wait; I think the demonstrated science is sufficient but this is a difference of criterion, not of fact.
Whether my metrology bias is leading me to under-weight the discovery character of IceCube (B021) or the quantum-matter case of B016.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with B014: none of Katori, Ye or their groups is a collaborator, mentor, student or Lund colleague. Disclosures unchanged: I am in the WACQT leadership, institutionally overlapping with Johansson at Chalmers, which would matter if B009 advanced; I have a general AMO and quantum-information background overlapping B008 and have co-authored with European quantum-memory groups, without a named candidate being a direct collaborator. My bias toward measurement science is declared and should be discounted for B014; Lindroth's proximity to the field is similar.
